meta.method: For each of the 240 claims in positions 241-480 (na-c-241..na-c-480) I read the statement, place, authority and from/to dates against every cited quote and its quote_check result, then grepped the cached page text in .cache/fetch for surrounding context wherever a date, place or detail was not in the quote itself (e.g. treaty dates, founding years, end bounds, locations). I judged support for the claim's core (polity, place, authority type, dates at stated precision), marking partially-verified when a bound or anchor was inferred from another event/claim rather than the cited text, rejected for items wholly before 1492, and unverified where the only citations were unfetchable (Canadian Encyclopedia pages return 403 to curl and are too large for WebFetch). Window-clamp start dates (1492, circa) for time-immemorial occupation were accepted as disclosed conventions. The catalogue was not edited.

na-c-419.note: DNR and Wikipedia: Shk'ituk't large Dena'ina village at the Kenai River mouth, ~1,000 residents; Dena'ina displaced Kachemak around 1000 AD.

na-c-420.note: DNR Alaska: Fort St. Nicholas built 1791 staffed by ~40 Russians and Creoles; Wikipedia: Dena'ina attack and 1838 smallpox killing half. 1786 date conflict noted.

na-c-421.note: Knik Tribe and Wikipedia: Kenaht'ana of Knik Arm, Dena'ina in Upper Cook Inlet for ~1,000 years; mid-1800s smallpox killed half.

na-c-422.note: Nez Perce Tribe and Wikipedia: Nimiipuu homeland across Idaho, Oregon, Washington; main village Kamiah at Clearwater. 1492 is a window clamp.

na-c-423.note: NPS: Young Joseph left the Wallowas in spring 1877 under threat of eviction; Wikipedia: region occupied 11,500+ years. 1492 is a window clamp; lake anchor approximate.

na-c-424.note: NPS: after the 1863 treaty Wallowa Valley left outside reservation, 90% reduction; treaty text dated 9 June 1863; Old Joseph refused to sign.

na-c-425.note: NPS Dug Bar: Chief Joseph's band forded the Snake on 31 May 1877 complying with demand to leave Wallowa homeland.

na-c-426.note: Nez Perce Tribe: 1863 treaty reduced reservation to ~750,000 acres; Wikipedia: government headquartered at Lapwai.

na-c-427.note: NPS: Weippe Prairie a summer root, berry and hunting ground; Lewis and Clark first contact mid-September 1805. Seasonal-range authority fits.

na-c-428.note: Yakama Nation: peoples lived in the area since the beginning of time; Union Gap in Ahtanum Ridge. 1492 is a window clamp; Union Gap point approximate.

na-c-429.note: Yakama Nation and HistoryLink: 9 June 1855 treaty cession, ratified 8 March 1859; acreage conflict (12M vs 6M) noted. Yakima city anchor approximate.

na-c-430.note: HistoryLink: 9 Nov 1855 Rains marched on Kamiakin at Union Gap; by 1858 Yakama lost 90% of traditional lands and were confined to a reservation.

na-c-431.note: Yakama Nation: the Yakama accepted their reservation after the war and still live there; rights reserved in the 1855 treaty. Toppenish-area point approximate.

na-c-432.note: CTUIR: Cayuse people in Columbia region 10,000+ years; Wikipedia: Whitman mission at Waiilatpu among the Cayuse. 1855 end is the treaty cession (claim 433). 1492 is a window clamp.

na-c-433.note: CTUIR and CRITFC: 6.4 million acres ceded for a reservation in the 1855 treaty; Cayuse ceded most traditional territory per Wikipedia.

na-c-434.note: Wikipedia: Cayuse share reservation and government with Umatilla and Walla Walla; CTUIR reserved off-reservation fishing rights.

na-c-435.note: Wikipedia and CTUIR: Umatilla along Umatilla and Columbia rivers with seasonal rounds from river lowlands to Blue Mountains. Town of Umatilla point approximate.

na-c-436.note: CTUIR and CRITFC: reservation from the 1855 treaty, now 172,000 acres, seat of the Confederated Tribes at Mission; acreage figures vary (disclosed).

na-c-437.note: Wikipedia: Walla Walla people along the Walla Walla River; CTUIR: 10,000+ years in the region. 1855 end is the treaty cession; 1492 is a window clamp.

na-c-438.note: Treaty text: signed at Camp Stevens in the Walla Walla Valley 9 June 1855; CTUIR: 6.4 million acres ceded for a reservation.

na-c-439.note: Wikipedia and CRITFC: Walla Walla share the reservation and government with Cayuse and Umatilla.

na-c-440.note: Wikipedia Bitterroot Salish: occupied Bitterroot Valley from the 1700s, mission built 1841 by request, forcibly moved 1891; NWE gives the October 1891 removal.

na-c-441.note: Treaty text and NWE: Hellgate treaty 16 July 1855 ceded ~20 million acres, Bitterroot Valley a conditional reservation. Hell Gate point approximate.

na-c-442.note: NWE: October 1891 Chief Charlot and remaining members marched sixty miles to the Flathead Reservation; Wikipedia: forcibly moved 1891.

na-c-443.note: CSKT and Wikipedia: Flathead Reservation established by Hellgate Treaty and home to the three tribes.

na-c-444.note: Coeur d'Alene Tribe: people on the lake shores for thousands of years; Wikipedia: reservation includes lower third of the lake. 1492 is a window clamp.

na-c-445.note: Wikipedia supports Rosalia/Steptoe Butte as Coeur d'Alene territory and Steptoe's May 1858 Pine Creek defeat; nothing says the area ceased to be theirs in 1858, so the end year is an event date.

na-c-446.note: Tribe: 8 Nov 1873 executive order established the reservation; Wikipedia: later reduced to 345,000 acres near Plummer (fuzzy quote). Acreage at establishment differs by source.

na-c-447.note: Spokane Tribe and Wikipedia: ancestral lands of ~3 million acres in NE Washington along Spokane and Columbia rivers, Spokane Falls area; 1881 end per reservation (claim 448).

na-c-448.note: Spokane Tribe: no treaty, defended country in 1858, 1881 reservation, 1887 agreement; Wikipedia: ceded most territory on accepting the reservation established 1881.

na-c-449.note: Spokane Tribe: President Hayes established the reservation in 1881; Wellpinit seat not in quotes but not load-bearing.

na-c-450.note: Wikipedia Palouse people: main village Palus at the Palouse-Snake junction below Palouse Falls; Lewis and Clark met the tribe October 1805 (first documentation).

na-c-451.note: NPS lists Palouse at the 1855 Walla Walla council and Wikipedia names them signatories of the 1855 treaty; post-1858 Yakama enrolment is not in the quotes but not load-bearing.

na-c-452.note: Wikipedia Western Shoshone: indigenous to the Great Basin, lands in the 1863 Ruby Valley treaty, Watatikka band at Ruby Valley. 1492 is a window clamp.

na-c-453.note: Wikipedia and digitreaties: Treaty of Ruby Valley concluded 1 Oct 1863; Shoshone allowed passage and posts but did not cede land; claims settlement later refused.

na-c-454.note: Wikipedia supports Cache Valley as traditional hunting ground and base of the Cache Valley Shoshone; the 1863 end is inferred from the massacre/treaty and some Shoshone remained.

na-c-455.note: Wikipedia: Cache Valley Shoshone practically wiped out at Bear River on 29 Jan 1863; Wyohistory gives at least 250 killed.

na-c-456.note: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes: reservation established by executive order 14 June 1867 as permanent home; Wikipedia: survivors settled at Fort Hall.

na-c-457.note: WyoHistory: 1863 Fort Bridger treaty specified ~44 million acre Eastern Shoshone homeland; Wikipedia Washakie concurs. End 1868 is the later treaty.

na-c-458.note: WyoHistory: 1868 treaty shrank the homeland to ~3.2 million acres centred on Wind River Valley; SBT lists the 1868 treaty.

na-c-459.note: Wikipedia and treaty text: Wind River Valley set apart in 1868, Shoshone longest precontact presence, Fort Washakie renamed 1878, shared with Arapaho.

na-c-460.note: Wikipedia: in 1872 the Shoshone agreed to sell part of the reservation to the U.S.

na-c-461.note: Wikipedia: Pyramid Lake people known as Kuyui Dukadu; reservation first set aside 1859; NPS notes Paiute living in the area. 1492 is a window clamp.

na-c-462.note: NPS, Nevada SHPO and Wikipedia: 1860 Pyramid Lake War over encroachment, ceasefire August 1860 with no treaty; NPS dates start 7 May 1860.

na-c-463.note: Wikipedia places the reservation along the Walker River and Northern Paiute in the Great Basin, but nothing readable dates the Agaidokado at Walker River back to 1492; Wovoka detail unchecked.

na-c-464.note: EBSCO and Wikipedia support Southern Paiute bands in the region incl. Nevada and a Las Vegas band; neither places the band at Las Vegas Springs, so the anchor is inferred.

na-c-465.note: EBSCO: 1873 Powell commission recommended consolidation on Uintah or the Moapa River Reservation, which was already established; Mormon settlement from 1850.

na-c-466.note: Forest Service and Wikipedia: Washoe at Lake Tahoe for at least 2,000 years, territory centred on the lake. 1492 is a window clamp.

na-c-467.note: Forest Service: 1859 Virginia City silver strike brought massive resource extraction, the first major disruption to Washoe life at the lake.

na-c-468.note: NPS and Klamath Tribes: Tule Lake, Lost River, Clear Lake, Butte Valley were Modoc homeland; end 1873 is war's end. 1492 is a window clamp.

na-c-469.note: Treaty text, Klamath Tribes and Wikipedia: 14 Oct 1864 treaty, 23 million acres, Modoc to give up Lost River/Tule Lake lands.

na-c-470.note: NPS gives the Modoc War as 29 Nov 1872 to 1 June 1873 and 150 people in the Stronghold for five months; those are war dates, not the dates the Stronghold was held, which are shorter.

na-c-471.note: NPS Lava Beds: twelve days after the 3 Oct 1873 hanging, 163 Modoc sent as prisoners to the Quapaw Agency; some returned to the Klamath Reservation in 1909.

na-c-472.note: Klamath Tribes: lived in the Klamath Basin from time beyond memory, six tribes; end 1864 is the treaty cession (claim 473). 1492 is a window clamp; basin point approximate.

na-c-473.note: Klamath Tribes: ceded more than 23 million acres in 1864 and entered the reservation era; treaty text concluded at Klamath Lake 14 Oct 1864.

na-c-474.note: Klamath Tribes history mentions the Agency and Fort Klamath, cattle ranching, and lumber sales under the reservation program; Wikipedia: 1864 treaty cession in return for the reservation.

na-c-475.note: Yurok Tribe: lived in over fifty villages across ancestral territory, Klamath-Trinity River lifeline. Requa anchor and 1492 clamp disclosed.

na-c-476.note: Yurok Tribe supports 1849 arrival of gold seekers and at least 75% dying by the end of the gold rush era; the 1855 end year is inferred from the reservation's creation.

na-c-477.note: Yurok Tribe: Federal Government established the Yurok Reservation in 1855, considerably smaller than ancestral territory.

na-c-478.note: Wikipedia: over 150 independent Chumash villages before the mission period; Santa Ynez Band reservation in the Santa Ynez Valley. Mission Santa Barbara is only a region anchor.

na-c-479.note: California Missions Foundation: Mission Santa Barbara founded 4 Dec 1786, ~4,000 Chumash buried; Wikipedia: Chumash moved to missions 1772-1817.

na-c-480.note: Wikipedia Chumash Revolt of 1824: La Purisima occupied until a Mexican unit forced surrender on 16 March; CMF Santa Ines page corroborates the revolt.
